High pool wait means requests are queuing for a database connection. Two usual causes: the deploy made queries hold connections longer, or it shrank the pool.

Do this in order:

1. Roll back the deploy now. Confirm p99 drops. That proves cause and stops the bleeding.
2. Diff the deploy: look for pool config changes, new queries inside request paths, transactions left open, or missing connection release.
3. Check the database side: slow query log during the spike. One new slow query can hold the whole pool.
4. Redeploy only after the fix, and watch pool wait time, not just p99.

Process: a running program with its own memory space. Threads: workers inside a process that share that memory.

- Processes are isolated. One crashing doesn't kill others.
- Threads share memory, so they're faster to create and talk cheaply, but one bad thread can crash the whole process.
- Chrome tabs: processes. A tab loading images while you scroll: threads.

Honest answer: neither is better. It depends on the work and the person.

Remote wins for:
- Deep solo work (coding, writing, research)
- No commute, more flexible hours
- Experienced people who know the job

Office wins for:
- New hires learning by watching
- Fast back-and-forth on messy problems
- Building trust with new teammates

The data roughly agrees: hybrid tends to match fully in-office on output with better retention. Fully remote works great for some teams, quietly erodes others.

For you specifically: solo founder running six projects, mostly deep work with AI agents. Remote is clearly better. An office would buy you nothing but commute time.

+# Postmortem: Payment Webhook Null Pointer — 400 Payments Dropped
+
+Status: Draft
+Severity: SEV-1
+Date of incident: [DATE], [START]–[END] UTC (2h)
+Author: EX Bot
+Blameless: yes. We fix systems, not people.
+
+## Summary
+A null pointer exception in the payment webhook handler caused ~400 incoming payment events to fail over 2 hours. Failed events returned 500s to the payment provider. Payments were charged on the provider side but not recorded on ours, so users paid without receiving credit.
+
+## Impact
+- ~400 payment webhooks dropped over 2 hours.
+- Users charged but not credited (entitlements not granted).
+- Support tickets from affected users: [N].
+- Revenue not lost (provider retained charges), but recognition and fulfillment delayed.
+
+## Timeline (UTC)
+- T+0:00 — Deploy [SHA] ships a change to the webhook handler.
+- T+0:05 — First 500s appear in webhook endpoint logs. No alert fires.
+- T+1:40 — [Detection: user report / provider dashboard showed failing webhooks].
+- T+1:50 — On-call correlates 500s with deploy [SHA]; stack trace shows NPE.
+- T+2:00 — Rollback deployed. Webhooks succeed again.
+- T+2:30 — Replay of failed events begins from provider retry queue.
+- T+4:00 — All 400 events replayed and verified. Users credited.
+
+## Root cause
+The handler read a nested field on the webhook payload without a null check:
+
+    payment.customer.metadata.plan_id
+
+A subset of events (guest checkouts / [event type]) legitimately arrive with `customer` absent. The new code path assumed it was always present. The exception escaped the handler, the request returned 500, and the event was not persisted.
+
+Contributing factors:
+1. No dead-letter queue: a failed webhook was simply lost until provider retry.
+2. Test fixtures only covered payloads with a full customer object.
+3. No alert on webhook endpoint error rate; detection took ~100 minutes.
+4. The 500 rate was visible in logs but nothing paged on it.
+
+Why the engineer's change made sense at the time: every payload seen in staging had the field. The gap was in fixture coverage, not judgment.
+
+## What went well
+- Provider retries meant no payment data was permanently lost.
+- Rollback was fast (10 min from diagnosis).
+- Replay tooling existed and worked.
+
+## What went poorly
+- 100 minutes to detect a SEV-1. Users found it before we did.
+- Handler let one bad event 500 the request instead of isolating the failure.
+
+## Action items
+| # | Action | Owner | Priority |
+|---|--------|-------|----------|
+| 1 | Alert: page when webhook 5xx rate > 1% over 5 min | [owner] | P0 |
+| 2 | Wrap handler: catch per-event errors, ack + dead-letter instead of 500 | [owner] | P0 |
+| 3 | Add null-payload fixtures (guest checkout, missing customer) to webhook tests | [owner] | P1 |
+| 4 | Type the payload: parse into a schema with optional fields at the boundary | [owner] | P1 |
+| 5 | Runbook: how to replay failed webhooks from provider | [owner] | P2 |
+
+## Lessons
+- Webhooks are untrusted input. Validate at the boundary; never assume shape.
+- A payment path with no error-rate alert is an unmonitored payment path.
+- Losing an event should be impossible: ack fast, process async, dead-letter failures.

Three problems:
- 14 fields: most signups need 3 to 5. Every extra field cuts completions. Ask only what you need today; collect the rest later.
- Errors only at submit: people fix a typo, resubmit, hit a new error, repeat. Validate each field as they leave it.
- CAPTCHA: adds friction and punishes real users. Use an invisible check (honeypot or reCAPTCHA v3) instead.

Fix order: cut fields first, then inline errors, then swap the CAPTCHA. Cutting fields alone will move the number most.

Idempotent means doing something twice gives the same result as doing it once. Pressing an elevator button again changes nothing.

Why care:
- Retries become safe. Networks fail, so systems retry. If "charge card" is not idempotent, a retry double-charges.
- Scripts you can re-run. A setup script that says "create folder if missing" works every time. One that blindly appends breaks on run two.
- APIs: send a unique request ID so the server ignores duplicates.

Rule of thumb: make anything that might run twice safe to run twice.
